subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The AM Signal Whose Envelope Pinched Shut
featured_title: THE AM SIGNAL WHOSE ENVELOPE PINCHED SHUT

presentation.challenge: The carrier was 5 V. The message amplitude was 6 V. The envelope detector stopped reproducing the message cleanly.

practice.primary_question: Why does conventional AM become overmodulated when the message amplitude exceeds the carrier amplitude?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Assuming a larger message amplitude always improves AM without checking whether the modulation index exceeds 1.

case_dna.target_misconception: In conventional AM, increasing message amplitude beyond the carrier amplitude only makes the transmitted signal stronger.
case_dna.why_plausible: Higher message amplitude does increase sideband amplitude, so it can look like a simple signal-strength improvement.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With Ac=5 V and Am=6 V, modulation index m=Am/Ac=1.2. Since m>1, the envelope crosses through zero and a simple envelope detector distorts the recovered signal.
case_dna.corrected_model: For standard AM with envelope detection, keep 0≤m≤1. The modulation index is m=Am/Ac for a single-tone message.

problem_statement: A conventional AM transmitter uses a 5 V carrier amplitude and a 6 V sinusoidal message amplitude. The technician expects the stronger message to improve the received audio, but an envelope detector produces severe distortion. Diagnose the modulation setting, calculate the modulation index, and choose a correction that restores valid envelope detection.
fixed_constraints: Conventional AM with envelope detection is retained

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The message got stronger. The recovered audio got worse.
gates.prompt: What limit did the modulation setting violate?

options.label: m = Am/Ac; if m>1, conventional AM is overmodulated
options.reason: A modulation index above 1 causes envelope reversal and distortion for simple envelope detection.

options.label: Any positive message amplitude is valid as long as a carrier exists
options.reason: Conventional AM has an envelope constraint for distortion-free envelope detection.

options.label: m = Ac/Am, so this signal has m<1
options.reason: For single-tone AM, m is message amplitude divided by carrier amplitude.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the modulation index
gates.prompt: With Am=6 V and Ac=5 V, what is the modulation index?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Observe the AM envelope
gates.result: The modulation index is 1.2, so the signal is 120% modulated.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the modulation setting
gates.prompt: Use m = Am/Ac = 6/5. Enter the modulation index.
gates.success: m = 1.2. Because m>1, the conventional AM envelope is overmodulated.
gates.hint: Divide message amplitude by carrier amplitude.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The envelope detector explains the distortion

cards.text: For m>1, the AM envelope crosses through zero and a simple envelope detector cannot reproduce the message without distortion.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the modulation review
report: C1. The carrier amplitude is 5 V.
C2. The message amplitude is 6 V.
C3. A larger message amplitude only increases modulation depth and cannot create envelope distortion.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores the m≤1 envelope constraint for conventional AM.

evidence_choices.label: m=6/5=1.2, so the signal is overmodulated
evidence_choices.reason: This directly identifies the violated AM condition.

correction.template: The modulation index is {m}; because it exceeds 1, the AM signal is overmodulated.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Restore valid envelope detection
gates.constraint: Keep the carrier amplitude at 5 V.

options.label: Reduce the message amplitude to 5 V or less
Increase the message amplitude to 7 V
Remove the carrier while keeping an envelope detector
options.reason: A conventional envelope detector requires the transmitted carrier/envelope structure.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the modulation-index rule
gates.prompt: A conventional AM signal has Ac=8 V and Am=4 V. What is m?

options.reason: Modulation index is a ratio, not the sum of amplitudes.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the AM correction
gates.confirmation: I confirm that conventional AM intended for envelope detection must keep the modulation index at or below 1.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: More message amplitude was assumed to be always beneficial.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Check m=Am/Ac and keep m≤1 for conventional AM envelope detection.

seo.seo_title: AM Modulation Index: Why 120% Modulation Distorts | FE E-035
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-035: a 5 V carrier with a 6 V message gives m=1.2 and overmodulates a conventional AM signal. Diagnose envelope distortion.
seo.excerpt: A stronger message signal can break conventional AM envelope detection when the modulation index exceeds 1.
seo.direct_answer: For single-tone conventional AM, the modulation index is m=Am/Ac. With a 6 V message and 5 V carrier, m=1.2, or 120%. Because m>1, the AM envelope is overmodulated and simple envelope detection produces distortion.
